The purpose of this page is to catalog new, interesting, and useful identities related to [[number theory|number-theoretic]] divisor sums, i.e., sums of an [[arithmetic function]] over the divisors of a [[natural number]] <math>n</math>, or equivalently the [[Dirichlet convolution]] of an arithmetic function <math>f(n)</math> with one:

<math display="block">g(n) := \sum_{d\mid n} f(d).</math>

These identities include applications to sums of an arithmetic function over just the proper prime divisors of <math>n</math>. 
We also define [[Periodic function|periodic]] variants of these divisor sums with respect to the [[greatest common divisor]] function in the form of

<math display="block">g_m(n) := \sum_{d\mid (m,n)} f(d),\ 1 \leq m \leq n</math>

Well-known inversion relations that allow the function <math>f(n)</math> to be expressed in terms of <math>g(n)</math> are provided by the [[Möbius inversion formula]]. 
Naturally, some of the most interesting examples of such identities result when considering the [[Average order of an arithmetic function|average order summatory functions]] over an arithmetic function <math>f(n)</math> defined as a divisor sum of another arithmetic function <math>g(n)</math>. Particular examples of divisor sums involving special [[arithmetic functions]] and special [[Dirichlet convolution]]s of arithmetic functions can be found on the following pages: 
[[Arithmetic function#Dirichlet convolutions|here]], [[Dirichlet convolution#Examples|here]], [[Arithmetic function#Miscellaneous|here]], [[Euler's totient function#Other formulae|here]], and [[Ramanujan's sum#Kluyver|here]].

==Average order sum identities==

===Interchange of summation identities===

The following identities are the primary motivation for creating this topic page. These identities do not appear to be well-known, or at least well-documented, and are extremely useful tools to have at hand in some applications. In what follows, we consider that <math>f,g,h,u,v: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}</math> are any prescribed [[arithmetic functions]] and that <math display="inline">G(x) := \sum_{n \leq x} g(n)</math> denotes the summatory function of <math>g(n)</math>. A more common special case of the first summation below is referenced [[Average order of an arithmetic function#Calculating mean values using Dirichlet series|here]].<ref>See also Section 3.10 of Apostol.</ref>

# <math>\sum_{n=1}^x v(n) \sum_{d\mid n} h(d) u\left(\frac{n}{d}\right) = \sum_{n=1}^x h(n) \sum_{k=1}^{\left\lfloor \frac{x}{n} \right\rfloor} u(k) v(nk) </math> 
# <math>
   \begin{align} 
   \sum_{n=1}^x \sum_{d\mid n} f(d) g\left(\frac{n}{d}\right) & = \sum_{n=1}^x f(n) G\left(\left\lfloor \frac{x}{n} \right\rfloor\right) 
   = \sum_{i=1}^x \left(\sum_{\left\lceil \frac{x+1}{i+1} \right\rceil \leq n \leq \left\lfloor \frac{x-1}{i} \right\rfloor} f(n)\right) G(i) + 
   \sum_{d\mid x} G(d) f\left(\frac{x}{d}\right) 
   \end{align} 
   </math> 
# <math>\sum_{d=1}^x f(d) \left(\sum_{r\mid (d,x)} g(r) h\left(\frac{d}{r}\right)\right) = \sum_{r\mid x} g(r) \left(\sum_{1 \leq d \leq x/r} h(d) f(rd)\right) </math> 
# <math>\sum_{m=1}^x \left(\sum_{d\mid(m,x)} f(d) g\left(\frac{x}{d}\right)\right) = \sum_{d\mid x} f(d) g\left(\frac{x}{d}\right) \cdot \frac{x}{d} </math> 
# <math>\sum_{m=1}^x \left(\sum_{d\mid (m,x)} f(d) g\left(\frac{x}{d}\right)\right) t^m = (t^x-1) \cdot \sum_{d\mid x} \frac{t^d f(d)}{t^d-1} g\left(\frac{x}{d}\right) </math>

In general, these identities are collected from the so-called "''rarities and b-sides''" of both well established and semi-obscure [[analytic number theory]] notes and techniques and the papers and work of the contributors. The identities themselves are not difficult to prove and are an exercise in standard manipulations of series inversion and divisor sums. Therefore, we omit their proofs here.

===The convolution method===

The '''convolution method''' is a general technique for estimating average order sums of the form

<math display="block">\sum_{n \leq x} f(n) \qquad\text{ or } \qquad \sum_{\stackrel{q \leq x}{q\text{ squarefree}}} f(q), </math>

where the [[multiplicative function]] ''f'' can be written as a convolution of the form <math>f(n) = (g \ast h)(n)</math> for suitable, application-defined [[arithmetic function]]s ''g'' and ''h''. A short survey of this method can be found [https://people.math.gatech.edu/~ecroot/convolution.pdf here].

A related technique is the use of the formula
<math display="block">\sum_{k=1}^n f(k) = \sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{xy=k}^{} g(x)h(y)
= \sum_{x=1}^a \sum_{y=1}^{n/x} g(x)h(y) + \sum_{y=1}^b \sum_{x=1}^{n/y} g(x)h(y) - \sum_{x=1}^a \sum_{y=1}^b g(x)h(y);</math>
this is known as the [[Dirichlet hyperbola method]].

==Periodic divisor sums==

An [[arithmetic function]] is ''periodic (mod k)'', or ''k''-periodic, if <math>f(n+k) = f(n)</math> for all <math>n \in \mathbb{N}</math>. Particular examples of ''k''-periodic number theoretic functions are the [[Dirichlet character]]s <math>f(n) = \chi(n)</math> modulo ''k'' and the [[greatest common divisor]] function <math>f(n) = (n, k)</math>. It is known that every ''k''-periodic arithmetic function has a representation as a ''finite'' discrete [[Fourier series]] of the form

<math display="block">f(n) = \sum_{m=1}^k a_k(m) e\left(\frac{mn}{k}\right), </math>

where the [[Fourier coefficients]] <math>a_k(m)</math> defined by the following equation are also ''k''-periodic:

<math display="block">a_k(m) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{n=1}^k f(n) e\left(-\frac{mn}{k}\right). </math>

We are interested in the following ''k''-periodic divisor sums:

<math display="block">s_k(n) := \sum_{d\mid (n,k)} f(d) g\left(\frac{k}{d}\right) = \sum_{m=1}^k a_k(m) e\left(\frac{mn}{k}\right). </math>

It is a fact that the Fourier coefficients of these divisor sum variants are given by the formula <ref>Section 27.10 in the ''NIST Handbook of Mathematical Functions'' (DLMF).</ref>

<math display="block">a_k(m) = \sum_{d\mid (m,k)} g(d) f\left(\frac{k}{d}\right) \frac{d}{k}. </math>

===Fourier transforms of the GCD===

We can also express the Fourier coefficients in the equation immediately above in terms of the [[Fourier transform]] of any function ''h'' at the input of <math>\operatorname{gcd}(n, k)</math> using the following result where <math>c_q(n)</math> is a [[Ramanujan sum]] (cf. [[Euler's totient function#Fourier transform|Fourier transform of the totient function]]):<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Schramm|first1=W.|title=The Fourier transform of functions of the greatest common divisors|journal=Integers|date=2008|volume=8}}</ref>

<math display="block">F_h(m, n) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} h((k,n)) e\left(-\frac{km}{n}\right) = (h \ast c_{\bullet}(m))(n). </math>

Thus by combining the results above we obtain that

<math display="block">a_k(m) = \sum_{d\mid(m,k)} g(d) f\left(\frac{k}{d}\right) \frac{d}{k} = \sum_{d\mid k} \sum_{r\mid d} f(r) g(d) c_{\frac{d}{r}}(m). </math>

==Sums over prime divisors==

Let the function <math>a(n)</math> denote the [[characteristic function]] of the [[primes]], i.e., <math>a(n) = 1</math> ''if and only if'' <math>n</math> is prime and is zero-valued otherwise. Then as a special case of the first identity in equation (1) in section [[Divisor sum identities#Interchange of summation identities|interchange of summation identities]] above, we can express the average order sums

<math display="block">\sum_{n=1}^x \sum_{\stackrel{p\mid n}{p\text{ prime}}} f(p) = \sum_{p=1}^x a(p) f(p) \left\lfloor \frac{x}{p} \right\rfloor = 
       \sum_{\stackrel{p=1}{p\text{ prime}}}^x  f(p) \left\lfloor \frac{x}{p} \right\rfloor. </math>

We also have an integral formula based on [[Abel's summation formula|Abel summation]] for sums of the form <ref>See Section 2.2 in {{cite arXiv|last1=Villarino|first1=M. B.|title=Mertens' Proof of Mertens' Theorem|date=2005|eprint=math/0504289 }}</ref>

<math display="block">\sum_{\stackrel{p=1}{p\text{ prime}}}^x f(p) = \pi(x) f(x) - \int_2^x \pi(t) f^{\prime}(t) dt \approx 
       \frac{x f(x)}{\log x} - \int_2^x \frac{t}{\log t} f^{\prime}(t) dt, </math>

where <math>\pi(x) \sim \frac{x}{\log x}</math> denotes the [[prime-counting function]]. Here we typically make the assumption that the function ''f'' is [[Continuous function|continuous]] and [[Differentiable function|differentiable]].

==Some lesser appreciated divisor sum identities==

We have the following divisor sum formulas for ''f'' any arithmetic function and ''g'' [[completely multiplicative]] where <math>\varphi(n)</math> is [[Euler's totient function]] and <math>\mu(n)</math> is the [[Möbius function]]:<ref>In respective order from Apostol's book: Exercise 2.29, Theorem 2.18, and Exercises 2.31-2.32</ref><ref>The first identity has a well-known [[Dirichlet series]] of the form <math>\sum_{n \geq 1} \frac{1}{n^s} \sum_{k=1}^n f(\operatorname{gcd}(n, k)) = \frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)} \sum_{n \geq 1} \frac{f(n)}{n^s}</math> catalogued in {{cite journal
 |first1      = Henry W.
 |last1       = Gould
 |first2      = Temba
 |last2       = Shonhiwa
 |title       = A catalogue of interesting Dirichlet series
 |journal     = Miss. J. Math. Sci.
 |volume      = 20
 |issue       = 1
 |year        = 2008
 |url         = http://www.math-cs.ucmo.edu/~mjms/2008-1p.html
 |url-status     = dead
 |archiveurl  = https://web.archive.org/web/20111002201720/http://www.math-cs.ucmo.edu/~mjms/2008-1p.html
 |archivedate = 2011-10-02
}}</ref>

# <math>\sum_{d\mid n} f(d) \varphi\left(\frac{n}{d}\right) = \sum_{k=1}^n f(\operatorname{gcd}(n, k)) </math> 
# <math>\sum_{d\mid n} \mu(d) f(d) = \prod_{\stackrel{p\mid n}{p\text{ prime}}} (1-f(p)) </math> 
# If ''f'' is multiplicative, ''g'' is completely multiplicative and satisfy, <math> f(p^{n+1})= f(p)f(p^n) - g(p)f(p^{n-1}), </math> for all primes ''p'' and <math> n \geq 1</math>, then, <math> f(m)f(n) = \sum_{d\mid (m,n)} g(d) f\left(\frac{mn}{d^2}\right). </math> <ref>Introduction to Analytic Number Theory, Apostol, Exercises 2.30 -2.31</ref>
# If ''f'' is [[completely multiplicative]] then the pointwise multiplication <math>\cdot</math> with a Dirichlet convolution yields <math>f \cdot (g \ast h) = (f \cdot g) \ast (f \cdot h)</math>.
# <math>\sum_{d^k\mid n} \mu(d) = \Biggl\{\begin{array}{ll} 0, & \text{ if } m^k\mid n \text{ for some } m>1; \\ 1, & \text{otherwise.}\end{array}</math>
# If <math>m \geq 1</math> and ''n'' has more than ''m'' [[prime omega function|distinct prime factors]], then <math>\sum_{d\mid n} \mu(d) \log^m(d) = 0.</math>

==The Dirichlet inverse of an arithmetic function==

We adopt the notation that <math>\varepsilon(n) = \delta_{n,1}</math> denotes the multiplicative identity of Dirichlet convolution so that <math> (\varepsilon \ast f)(n) = (f \ast \varepsilon)(n) = f(n)</math> for any arithmetic function ''f'' and <math>n \geq 1</math>. The '''Dirichlet inverse''' of a function ''f'' satisfies <math>(f \ast f^{-1})(n) = (f^{-1} \ast f)(n) = \varepsilon(n)</math> for all <math>n \geq 1</math>. There is a well-known recursive convolution formula for computing the [[Dirichlet inverse]] <math>f^{-1}(n)</math> of a function ''f'' by induction given in the form of <ref>See Section 2.7 of Apostol's book for a proof.</ref>

<math display="block">f^{-1}(n) = \Biggl\{\begin{array}{ll} \frac{1}{f(1)}, & \text{ if } n = 1; \\ -\frac{1}{f(1)} \sum_{\stackrel{d\mid n}{d>1}} f(d) f^{-1}\left(\frac{n}{d}\right), & \text{ if } n>1. \end{array}</math>

For a fixed function ''f'', let the function <math>f_{\pm}(n) := (-1)^{\delta_{n,1}} f(n) = \Biggl\{\begin{matrix} -f(1), & \text{ if } n=1; \\ f(n), & \text{ if } n>1 \end{matrix}</math>

Next, define the following two multiple, or nested, convolution variants for any fixed arithmetic function ''f'':

<math display="block">
  \begin{align} 
  \widetilde{\operatorname{ds}}_{j,f}(n) & := \underbrace{\left(f_{\pm} \ast f \ast \cdots \ast f\right)}_{j\text{ times}}(n) \\ 
  \operatorname{ds}_{j,f}(n) & := \Biggl\{\begin{array}{ll} f_{\pm}(n), & \text{ if } j=1; \\ \sum\limits_{\stackrel{d\mid n}{d>1}} f(d) \operatorname{ds}_{j-1,f}(n/d), & \text{ if } j > 1. \end{array} 
  \end{align} 
</math>

The function <math>D_f(n)</math> by the equivalent pair of summation formulas in the next equation is closely related to the [[Dirichlet inverse]] for an arbitrary function ''f''.<ref name="MSGENLSFACTTHMS">{{cite arXiv|last1=M. Merca and M. D. Schmidt|title=Factorization Theorems for Generalized Lambert Series and Applications|date=2017|pages=13–20|eprint=1712.00611|class=math.NT}}</ref>

<math display="block">D_f(n) := \sum_{j=1}^n \operatorname{ds}_{2j,f}(n) = \sum_{m=1}^{\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right\rfloor} \sum_{i=0}^{2m-1} \binom{2m-1}{i} (-1)^{i+1} \widetilde{\operatorname{ds}}_{i+1,f}(n)</math>

In particular, we can prove that <ref>This identity is proved in an unpublished manuscript by M. D. Schmidt which will appear on ArXiv in 2018.</ref>

<math display="block">f^{-1}(n) = \left(D + \frac{\varepsilon}{f(1)}\right)(n).</math>

A table of the values of <math>D_f(n)</math> for <math>2 \leq n \leq 16</math> appears below. This table makes precise the intended meaning and interpretation of this function as the signed sum of all possible multiple ''k''-convolutions of the function ''f'' with itself.

Let <math>p_k(n) := p(n-k)</math> where ''p'' is the [[Partition function (number theory)]]. Then there is another expression for the Dirichlet inverse given in terms of the functions above and the coefficients of the [[q-Pochhammer symbol]] for <math> n > 1</math> given by <ref name="MSGENLSFACTTHMS" />

<math display="block">f^{-1}(n) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[(p_k \ast \mu)(n) + (p_k \ast D_f \ast \mu)(n)\right] \times [q^{k-1}] \frac{(q; q)_{\infty}}{1-q}.</math>
